newsitem.title: UK: Row over Sinn Fein contacts clouds N.Irish talks.
newsitem.headline: Row over Sinn Fein contacts clouds N.Irish talks.

text.p: Northern Irish peace talks resume on Tuesday under a cloud after a row over Britain's acknowledgement that it had been in contact with the IRA's political wing, Sinn Fein.
Britain and Ireland broke off contacts with Sinn Fein after the IRA shot dead two policemen in an ambush a month ago.
The new preliminary contacts were designed to encourage Sinn Fein to persuade its IRA allies to call a new ceasefire -- the price for Sinn Fein's entry into the peace talks proper.
Northern Ireland Secretary Mo Mowlam said on Monday her civil servants had been in touch with Sinn Fein by telephone and in writing.
The admission, after the news was broken by the Irish Times, infuriated Protestant unionists loyal to British rule who said they had been misled by previous denials.
"Any private clarification is in fact a form of negotiation," said Ulster Unionist leader David Trimble.

Saying he was pressing for a House of Commons statement by Mowlam, Trimble added: "It would now be appropriate for the secretary of state to come to the House (of Commons) and to explain why she misled the house in the way that she did."
Mowlam said Sinn Fein had been answered so that it could not blame Britain's ban on preliminary contacts for the IRA's refusal to end its war against British rule.
"Tony Blair and I have made clear all along that what's important is that Sinn Fein cannot give any excuse that we have not clarified our position", she said.
Mowlam also insisted that the renewed contacts were initiated by Sinn Fein.
But the admission soured the atmosphere before Tuesday's resumption of the peace talks, dimming hopes of progress in the slow-moving process, and damaging Mowlam's standing further.

Mowlam, who was welcomed with genuine warmth when she took over after Labour's May 1 election victory, angered nationalists by her decision to allow the Protestant Orange Order to stage their annual parade through a Catholic area of Portadown.
The latest admission of contacts with Sinn Fein has added unionist anger to the nationalist bitterness.
One of the key topics on which Sinn Fein wants clarification is the question of "decommissioning" or disarming the IRA, which has bogged down the talks since their start in June 1996.
Sinn Fein and the IRA say the surrender of guerrilla weapons should be the last item on the talks agenda.
Britain and Ireland, co-sponsors of the talks, say the republican guerrillas should hand over some weapons as the talks progress to show good faith and build confidence.

This has angered unionists who fear London is going out of its way to get Sinn Fein to the talks to try and force through a dilution of the province's British sovereignty. The IRA, they argue, has no intention of giving up its weapons.
Mowlam's acknowledgement came less than 24 hours after police found a huge cache of home-made explosive in the staunchly Irish nationalist city of Londonderry.
Mitchel McLaughlin, the Sinn Fein chairman, told the BBC earlier that further, similar bombs were inevitable unless Britain eased its entry into the peace talks.
